entities.summary:
The Suda is a Byzantine lexicon created by various authors around 1000 AD. This comprehensive encyclopedia of the Byzantine era was a key source of information for scholars during the Middle Ages.

It contained extensive knowledge on various fields, including grammar, literature, mythology, and history. The Suda's most famous contributor, John Tzetzes, wrote about the gods of Greek mythology and provided detailed descriptions of their roles in mythological tales.

The Suda played a crucial role in preserving ancient texts and transmitting knowledge from the classical period to the Byzantine era. Its significance extends beyond its own historical context, as it has influenced later scholarly works on Byzantine culture and language.

One striking statistic about the Suda is that over 2,000 of its entries have been preserved in modern manuscripts, making it a valuable resource for historians studying Byzantine literature and linguistics.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Suda (Greek: Σοῦδα, also written Suidas, though the latter name is a misreading of the title — suda may derive from the Byzantine Greek word for 'fortress' or 'stronghold', σοῦδα) is a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopaedia, composed c. 970–975 CE under the reign of Emperor John I Tzimiskes (r. 969–976 CE) or possibly under Basil II (r. 976–1025 CE). It contains approximately 30,000 entries arranged alphabetically, covering a vast range of subjects: lexicography (word definitions, grammatical notes, etymologies), biography (entries on hundreds of ancient and Byzantine authors, rulers, and historical figures), literary criticism (quotations from lost works, assessments of authors' styles), historical summaries, mythological notes, and theological discussions. The Suda is the largest and most comprehensive Byzantine encyclopaedia and one of the most important reference works for Greek antiquity.

The Suda's entries draw on an extraordinary range of earlier sources — many now lost — including lexica (the Hesychius lexicon, the Etymologicum Magnum), historical collections (the excerpts from ancient historians compiled under Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos), biographies (the Onomatologos of Hesychius of Miletus), and a wide range of patristic and classical literature. The Suda's biographical entries — on ancient Greek poets, philosophers, historians, orators, and later Byzantine figures — are often the sole surviving source of information about authors whose works are lost, and its quotations preserve fragments of ancient texts (tragedies, comedies, poetry, prose) that would otherwise be completely unknown.

The Suda is a crucial tool for classical scholars because of its preservation of otherwise-lost information about ancient Greek literature and history. While its compilation is uneven — some entries are detailed and accurate, others are brief or confused — the Suda's role as a repository of the accumulated learning of the Byzantine scholarly tradition makes it an indispensable reference work. Its significance lies in its ability to bring together disparate knowledge areas under one roof, showcasing the intellectual curiosity and learning of the Byzantine scholars.

The Suda was compiled during a time of great cultural and scientific transformation in the Byzantine Empire, with the inclusion of works by prominent thinkers such as Aristotle and Galen. This lexicographic masterpiece not only reflects the intellectual pursuits of its creators but also provides valuable insights into the evolution of knowledge and ideas during this period.

As a testament to the enduring power of human curiosity and ingenuity, the Suda continues to captivate scholars and historians today, offering a unique window into the intellectual landscape of medieval Byzantium.
